The entire page renders as near-black text on a very dark burgundy background in both supplied screenshots. The brand name, navigation, headline, body copy and contact details are technically present but visually difficult to read.
dailyQueue.evidence: Desktop and mobile screenshots show extremely low contrast across all visible text. The page is dominated by an almost uniform dark field, with no clearly legible visual hierarchy.
dailyQueue.expected: A premium property site should establish immediate readability through deliberate contrast, refined typography, whitespace and strong visual anchors. Luxury styling can be restrained, but it cannot compromise legibility.
dailyQueue.location: Global page styling, especially header and hero
dailyQueue.observed: The first viewport feels broken or unfinished rather than editorial, aspirational or credible. The primary message is effectively inaccessible at a glance.
dailyQueue.recommendation: Correct the foreground/background contrast first. Use a clearly legible light-on-dark or dark-on-light system, verify contrast on every text style, and establish distinct treatments for the logo, navigation, H1, supporting copy and calls to action.
dailyQueue.title: First-viewport content is effectively unreadable

dailyQueue.detail: The homepage does not visually demonstrate the core product: properties for sale or rent in Écija. It presents an abstract text introduction without showing homes, spaces, locations or current inventory.
dailyQueue.evidence: The screenshot contains no visible property imagery or listing modules. The objective scan reports imageCount 0 and only 57 words on the document.
dailyQueue.expected: Premium real estate positioning requires the actual inventory and local market to be the first-viewport signal, with high-quality photography, property type, location and key facts visible immediately.
dailyQueue.location: Homepage hero and content immediately below it
dailyQueue.observed: A visitor cannot assess the quality, style or relevance of the agency's portfolio without navigating elsewhere, and the page provides no emotional or commercial reason to continue.
dailyQueue.recommendation: Lead with a curated property discovery module: large, high-quality local imagery, price, type, area, location and availability. Add a clear route into the complete inventory while preserving a restrained editorial composition.
dailyQueue.title: The homepage does not showcase the real estate offering

dailyQueue.detail: There is no meaningful enquiry mechanism in the homepage experience. The primary conversion path appears to be a generic Contacto link, with no visible form, property-specific enquiry action, phone action or contextual lead capture.
dailyQueue.evidence: The objective scan reports formCount 0, primaryCtaCount 1 and only one contact signal, the generic Contacto link. bookingSignalCount is 0.
dailyQueue.expected: The critical journey is property enquiry. Reference-quality execution gives visitors a low-friction way to request information, arrange a viewing or speak to the agency, ideally from both the homepage and each property detail page.
dailyQueue.observed: The user must make an additional navigation decision before they can enquire, and the CTA does not communicate what happens after clicking.
dailyQueue.recommendation: Add a prominent, specific CTA such as “Ver inmuebles” plus a secondary “Solicitar información” or “Concertar visita”. Include a short enquiry form with property, name, phone/email and preferred contact method, alongside click-to-call contact on mobile.
dailyQueue.title: The primary property-enquiry journey is underdeveloped

dailyQueue.detail: Property discovery is not available as an immediate workflow. The visible page offers no search controls, category entry points, featured inventory, or summary of available stock.
dailyQueue.evidence: The screenshots show only text navigation and introductory copy. The scan identifies internal links to /inmuebles but no form controls and no visible discovery interface on the homepage.
dailyQueue.expected: Visitors should be able to start browsing by intent, such as buying, renting, property type, area or budget, with a clear result count and useful filters on the inventory page.
dailyQueue.observed: “Inmuebles” is a destination link rather than a useful discovery step. The page does not help users understand what is available or how to narrow the search.
dailyQueue.recommendation: Add featured or latest properties to the homepage and make the inventory route explicit. Provide filters for operation, type, municipality, price and bedrooms, with strong mobile controls and persistent query state.
dailyQueue.title: Property discovery is reduced to a bare navigation link

dailyQueue.detail: The supplied page has no visual assets and therefore cannot deliver the editorial or aspirational qualities expected from premium real estate. The absence is especially damaging because property imagery is the primary way visitors evaluate fit and perceived value.
dailyQueue.evidence: The objective scan reports imageCount 0. Both screenshots show a flat background with no property photography, location imagery, floor plans, maps or branded visual detail.
dailyQueue.expected: Use real, well-lit property photography with consistent art direction and thoughtful crops. Imagery should reveal the actual homes and local environment rather than act as generic decoration.
dailyQueue.location: Homepage hero and property discovery content
dailyQueue.observed: The experience feels like a text placeholder or incomplete prototype, not a premium agency storefront.
dailyQueue.recommendation: Commission or curate a small set of authentic Écija property images. Use one strong hero property or local architectural image, then support it with a disciplined listing grid and consistent image ratios.
dailyQueue.title: No imagery supports the premium real-estate promise

dailyQueue.detail: The design language does not currently communicate premium real estate. The restrained burgundy background could support a sophisticated identity, but the execution lacks the contrast, composition, imagery, spacing and detail needed to make it feel intentional.
dailyQueue.evidence: The screenshots show a largely empty monochrome page with low-contrast text and no property media. The visible element count is only 22, and the page has no apparent visual content system.
dailyQueue.expected: Premium should feel calm and selective, with strong art direction, precise typography, generous but purposeful spacing, clear content sequencing and tangible evidence of quality.
dailyQueue.observed: The page reads closer to an unstyled or failed-render state than a finished luxury brand experience.
dailyQueue.recommendation: Rebuild the first viewport around one clear composition: legible brand/navigation, a property-led visual, a direct value proposition, and a high-intent CTA. Follow with inventory, local expertise and proof rather than leaving most of the viewport empty.
dailyQueue.title: The visual execution sits below the stated positioning

issues.detail: The primary visual asset does not convincingly show the product being rented. On desktop, the hero is almost entirely black and the featured vehicle is not visually legible; on mobile, the upper image is heavily blurred and reads as abstract scenery rather than a premium car photograph.
issues.evidence: Desktop screenshot shows a near-black hero with no inspectable vehicle image. Mobile screenshot shows a blurred, indistinct image occupying the full top section before the headline.
issues.expected: Reference-quality luxury rental sites make the vehicle immediately inspectable through sharp, high-resolution photography with controlled crop, lighting and enough contrast to communicate model, finish and desirability in the first viewport.
issues.location: Homepage hero, desktop and mobile first viewport
issues.observed: The site communicates luxury primarily through typography and darkness, while the actual rental inventory is visually absent or obscured.
issues.recommendation: Replace the hero background with a sharp, editorial vehicle image or short product-led video. Preserve the dark art direction with a controlled overlay, but keep the car silhouette, bodywork and model identity clearly visible. Use a deliberate responsive crop rather than a blurred mobile fallback.
issues.title: The hero does not sell the cars

issues.detail: The booking interaction is framed as an availability check, but the site does not visibly offer a true online reservation path or booking signal.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports bookingSignalCount: 0. The visible flow is date fields plus vehicle selection and the note: “Availability and final rental terms are confirmed with Mfinity via WhatsApp.”
issues.expected: A high-converting rental journey should make the next step explicit: either a genuine availability and reservation flow with clear confirmation states, or a highly structured enquiry flow that captures contact details, dates, vehicle and delivery needs without ambiguity.
issues.location: Homepage availability form and top-right “RENT ONLINE” CTA
issues.observed: “RENT ONLINE” suggests transactional booking, while the visible experience ultimately routes customers to a manual WhatsApp confirmation.
issues.recommendation: Align the CTA language with the actual capability, or implement the promised reservation journey. For a manual model, label it “CHECK AVAILABILITY” or “REQUEST A QUOTE,” then collect name, phone/email, dates, selected vehicle, delivery location and preferred contact method in one clear flow with a confirmation state.
issues.title: The booking promise and actual flow are misaligned

issues.detail: The first screen establishes an aspirational mood but does not provide enough immediate product evidence for a luxury car rental customer comparing vehicles.
issues.evidence: The desktop hero card names a Ferrari 488 Spyder and shows €1,400/day, but the car itself is not visible. The mobile first viewport contains no visible vehicle card or vehicle photography before the enquiry controls.
issues.expected: The first viewport should pair the positioning with a clearly visible vehicle, model, starting rate and a direct path to check dates or reserve that specific car.
issues.location: Homepage hero and featured vehicle module
issues.observed: Users must rely on the headline, a model name and a form to understand the actual fleet offering.
issues.recommendation: Make the featured car a real visual anchor in the hero, keep model and starting price adjacent to the image, and make the featured card's reserve action open a vehicle-specific enquiry with the selected model prefilled.
issues.title: Product discovery is subordinate to the art direction

issues.detail: Pricing clarity is incomplete for a customer who needs to make a rental decision. One featured rate is visible, but the broader fleet and rental terms are not easy to compare from the primary journey.
issues.evidence: The hero card exposes €1,400/day for the Ferrari 488 Spyder and mentions a €7,000 deposit, while the availability form defaults to “Any Mfinity car.” No comparable rates are visible in the supplied screenshots.
issues.expected: Reference execution gives customers enough pricing context to shortlist: per-day starting rates or transparent quote logic, deposit information, inclusions, duration rules and meaningful explanation of what changes the final price.
issues.location: Homepage featured vehicle and collection entry points
issues.observed: The single high price may create uncertainty about the rest of the fleet and forces users toward an enquiry before they can compare options.
issues.recommendation: Show consistent starting prices on vehicle cards and detail pages, state whether rates vary by duration or season, and surface deposit, mileage, insurance and delivery inclusions near the booking decision.
issues.title: Fleet pricing is not sufficiently comparable

issues.detail: The experience has no visible trust layer supporting a high-value rental decision. The presentation is polished but does not provide proof that the company is established, reliable or operationally clear.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports trustSignalCount: 0. The supplied screenshots show no reviews, fleet guarantees, insurance statement, company credentials, delivery promise, physical presence or customer proof.
issues.expected: Luxury rental references use restrained but concrete reassurance close to the enquiry action, such as verified reviews, insured fleet, concierge delivery coverage, transparent deposit policy and recognizable local operating details.
issues.location: Homepage, especially around the hero form and contact section
issues.observed: Customers are asked to submit dates and continue through WhatsApp without visible evidence reducing perceived risk.
issues.recommendation: Add a compact, factual trust band near the booking form and repeat the most relevant proof on vehicle detail pages. Include verifiable review content, insurance and deposit policy, service area, delivery terms and company/legal identity rather than generic claims.
issues.title: High-value conversion lacks visible proof

issues.detail: The homepage navigation and primary actions are visually restrained to the point that hierarchy is weaker than it should be for a reservation-led site.
issues.evidence: The desktop header places “CARS,” “ABOUT US” and “CONTACT” as small centered links, with the main brand mark not visibly prominent. The hero presents both “EXPLORE COLLECTION,” “CHECK AVAILABILITY” and a separate “RESERVE NOW” card action.
issues.expected: A premium interface can remain minimal while still making one primary action unmistakable and keeping brand, inventory and booking hierarchy immediately scannable.
issues.location: Desktop header and hero action group
issues.observed: Several actions compete, while the brand and reservation route have comparatively little visual ownership.
issues.recommendation: Give Mfinity a clear persistent wordmark, designate one primary booking action, and make secondary discovery actions visually quieter. Ensure the featured vehicle CTA and hero form reinforce the same next step instead of creating parallel routes.
issues.title: Minimalism weakens action hierarchy

issues.detail: The mobile hero spends substantial first-viewport space on a low-information image before presenting the car rental proposition and controls.
issues.evidence: The mobile screenshot shows approximately the first 460px occupied by a blurred image, followed by the brand and large headline. The vehicle selection and date form then extend well below the fold.
issues.expected: Mobile vehicle discovery should expose the proposition and a credible vehicle signal immediately, with the booking control arranged so users can reach a meaningful next step without excessive vertical scanning.
issues.observed: The initial screen is visually atmospheric but delays both product recognition and actionable rental context.
issues.recommendation: Reduce the image's vertical dominance, use a sharp car-led crop, and bring model/rate or a compact “view fleet” action into the first screen. Keep the date form accessible, but use progressive disclosure if its full height pushes the product signal too far down.
issues.title: Mobile first-viewport sequencing is inefficient

issues.detail: The interface relies heavily on near-black backgrounds, gray type and thin borders, which creates a strong mood but reduces tonal range and can make the experience feel like a stylized template rather than a distinctly local luxury brand.
issues.evidence: Both screenshots are dominated by black surfaces, muted gray typography and fine outlined controls. The only strong contrast is the white availability button and mobile CTA block.
issues.expected: Reference-quality luxury direction uses restraint with deliberate material contrast: premium imagery, selective highlights, varied dark tones, and distinctive details tied to the location or fleet.
issues.observed: The visual language is polished but generic and dependent on darkness to imply luxury; it does not yet express Marbella, Puerto Banus or Mfinity-specific character.
issues.recommendation: Introduce a more intentional material palette and brand signature through sharper image treatment, controlled warm or metallic accents, stronger vehicle-specific compositions and locally relevant editorial details. Keep the restraint, but make the source of distinction visible.
issues.title: The art direction is polished but generic

issues.detail: The sticky mobile actions provide useful reachability, but “WHATSAPP” and “RENT A CAR” do not clearly communicate the distinct outcomes or preserve the selected booking context.
issues.evidence: The mobile screenshot ends with two large fixed-looking actions labeled “WHATSAPP” and “RENT A CAR.” The scan also identifies contact signals but no booking signal.
issues.expected: Persistent mobile actions should map cleanly to the two highest-value tasks, such as “Check availability” and “WhatsApp concierge,” and should retain vehicle/date selections when possible.
issues.observed: The bar repeats a generic rental command while the actual workflow is an enquiry, creating uncertainty about what tapping each option will do.
issues.recommendation: Rename the actions around outcomes, make one primary, and ensure both routes carry the selected vehicle and dates into the destination. Add a visible confirmation or handoff state after WhatsApp initiation.
issues.title: Mobile sticky CTAs are too generic

issues.detail: The copy is confident and stylistically consistent, but some language is broad luxury marketing rather than decision-supporting rental content.
issues.evidence: The headline is “Luxury in every kilometer.” and supporting copy says “Supercars, performance cars and premium mobility for Marbella and the Costa del Sol.” The visible form only explains that final terms are confirmed via WhatsApp.
issues.expected: Luxury positioning should be supported by concrete local and operational information: delivery areas, lead time, rental duration, included mileage, concierge service and what customers can expect after submitting dates.
issues.location: Hero copy and booking helper text
issues.observed: The tone establishes aspiration but leaves important practical questions unanswered at the moment of intent.
issues.recommendation: Keep the concise headline, then add a compact factual line near the form covering response time, Marbella/Puerto Banus delivery, minimum rental duration and the main inclusions. Replace vague “premium mobility” phrasing with specific service proof where possible.
issues.title: Aspirational copy outweighs rental guidance

issues.detail: The visible positioning targets Marbella and the Costa del Sol, but the supplied experience does not show enough Puerto Banus-specific service detail to substantiate the niche claim.
issues.evidence: The hero mentions Marbella and Costa del Sol, and the bottom label says “Nueva Andalucia · Marbella.” No visible delivery zones, pickup points, concierge service or Puerto Banus operating details appear in the screenshots.
issues.expected: A locally focused luxury rental brand should make its service geography actionable, especially where delivery and handover are major purchase considerations.
issues.location: Homepage location messaging and enquiry context
issues.observed: Location is used as a tagline rather than as useful service information.
issues.recommendation: Add concise delivery and collection coverage for Marbella, Puerto Banus, Nueva Andalucia and nearby areas, including whether delivery is complimentary, available on request or priced separately.
issues.title: Local relevance is stated more than demonstrated

aiReview.summary: Mfinity has a credible premium visual foundation, but the experience currently sells atmosphere more effectively than it sells a rentable fleet. The most important gap is product visibility: the hero car is obscured on desktop and blurred on mobile, so the first impression does not deliver the vehicle photography expected in this niche. Conversion is also less direct than the “RENT ONLINE” promise suggests: the scan records no booking signal and the visible path ends in manual WhatsApp confirmation. Add sharp, inspectable vehicle imagery, align CTA language with the real enquiry capability, expose comparable pricing and rental terms, and add concrete trust and local-service proof. These changes would raise both perceived value and reservation confidence more than further visual polish.
strengths: The brand has a clear luxury-car-rental premise and a strong Marbella/Costa del Sol association.
The large typographic system creates a confident editorial tone and gives the homepage a recognizable visual direction.
The availability form is present in the hero, keeping dates and vehicle selection close to the primary intent.
The interface is restrained, responsive and free of visible layout breakage; the objective scan confirms strong performance, accessibility, metadata and link robustness.
The mobile layout preserves the main proposition and form controls without horizontal overflow.

issues.detail: The primary journey is to visit or contact, yet the homepage routes the user into discovery or a generic contact page rather than resolving the visit decision in place.
issues.evidence: The scan records 0 booking signals and only 4 contact signals, all of which are either a generic “Contacto” link or an email link. The hero CTA says “Visítanos hoy,” but the supplied viewport contains no address, map, phone/WhatsApp, opening-hours status, or directions action.
issues.expected: A reference-quality local hospitality homepage makes the visit decision immediate: exact Puerto Banús location, today's opening hours, and a one-tap route/contact action should be present at the first conversion moment.
issues.observed: The hero establishes Marbella and Puerto Banús as context, but it does not provide the practical information required to act on “Visítanos hoy.”
issues.recommendation: Turn “Visítanos hoy” into a specific visit module or anchored section with full address, hours including today’s status, Google/Apple Maps directions, and a direct phone or WhatsApp option. Retain the contact page as a secondary route.
issues.title: Visit CTA lacks the operational information needed to convert local intent

issues.detail: The positioning is elegantly stated but insufficiently proven for a premium sugar-free pâtisserie, leaving the most commercially important claim largely as brand language.
issues.evidence: The hero headline is “No sugar. Same taste.” and the supporting copy says “pastelería artesanal” and “más consciente.” The scan finds 0 trust signals across 439 words. The visible hero product case is distant and its individual products are not inspectable.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution pairs the promise with concise, credible proof: ingredient philosophy, relevant dietary/allergen guidance, chef credentials or method, signature products, reviews/press/awards where genuine, and close product evidence.
issues.location: Homepage hero and initial discovery flow
issues.observed: The message is memorable, but visitors must accept the central taste-and-quality claim without visible reasons to believe it.
issues.recommendation: Introduce a compact proof layer immediately below the hero: a signature-selection image set with named products, a specific explanation of the sugar-free approach, and only verified trust signals. Link this directly to the menu rather than relying on broad concept copy.
issues.title: The central sugar-free promise is not substantiated visually or commercially

issues.detail: The hero photograph communicates venue quality, but its crop and overlay prioritize atmosphere over the pâtisserie itself.
issues.evidence: In both supplied screenshots, much of the frame is ceiling, shelving, furniture, and a large text block. The product display occupies a narrow, partially obscured band; on mobile, the crop further favors cabinetry and the orange drink over clearly legible pastries. The dark overlay reduces detail in the display case.
issues.expected: For a premium pâtisserie, the first viewport should make the food look exceptional at a glance while still giving enough venue context to support the destination experience.
issues.observed: The image reads as a polished cafe interior before it reads as an appetizing premium pastry offer.
issues.recommendation: Use a dedicated mobile crop or alternate first-frame image with one or two hero products sharply visible, natural color and texture preserved, and the venue used as secondary context. Reduce or locally position the overlay so it does not mute the display.
issues.title: Hero imagery under-delivers on product appetite

issues.detail: Navigation and action styling are visually refined but do not form a consistent interaction system.
issues.evidence: The automated scan reports an inconsistent button ratio of 0.3077. In the desktop hero, “Descubrir la carta” is a filled rectangular control while “Visítanos hoy” is an underlined text link; the top-right “Contacto” is an outlined pill. On mobile, the primary CTA becomes materially wider and heavier than the nearby secondary action.
issues.expected: A reference-quality site uses a deliberate hierarchy with one recognizable primary action treatment, one secondary treatment, and a clear rationale for navigation controls.
issues.location: Homepage header and hero, desktop and mobile
issues.observed: The user can identify actions, but three different CTA languages compete in the first viewport and make the hierarchy feel less authored.
issues.recommendation: Standardize primary, secondary, and utility-action styles across the header and hero. Reserve the strongest filled treatment for the single conversion priority, use one quieter secondary treatment, and make header contact consistent with that hierarchy.
issues.title: CTA hierarchy is diluted by inconsistent button treatments

issues.detail: Three text navigation links are marginally below the conventional 44px minimum width, creating avoidable precision demands for a key mobile audience.
issues.evidence: The scan identifies 3 tiny tap targets out of 26: “Carta” at 42.1px wide, “Eric” at 29.2px wide, and “Legal” at 43.1px wide; each is 44px tall. The mobile screenshot shows a compact navigation pattern, making deliberate target sizing particularly important.
issues.expected: Every interactive target should provide a comfortably tappable hit area, independently of short label length.
issues.observed: Short-label links visually occupy only the width of their text and are easy to miss-touch despite adequate height.
issues.recommendation: Apply minimum inline hit areas of at least 44px by 44px, with appropriate spacing between adjacent links. Preserve the visual compactness by expanding invisible padding rather than enlarging text.
issues.title: Short mobile links have undersized tap areas

aiReview.summary: Zùsto Café presents above-average premium hospitality craft, with a convincing editorial direction and a fast, technically clean first impression. It is not reference quality yet because the experience spends its strongest viewport on an unproven promise and a venue-led image while the critical visit path lacks practical action information. More product evidence, credible proof of the sugar-free proposition, and an immediate directions/hours/contact layer would materially improve both perceived value and conversion.
strengths: The hero has strong immediate polish: restrained editorial typography, a credible real venue image, and a clear sugar-free proposition rather than generic cafe messaging.
The desktop and mobile compositions retain coherent brand character; the mobile layout is not simply a shrunken desktop and maintains legible hierarchy.

The visible page supports core discovery with clear routes to concept, menu, founder, visit, and contact, while technical scan results show no broken links, console errors, overflow, or major performance friction.
Location is established early through Puerto Banús/Marbella language, which aligns the site with destination-driven local discovery.

issues.title: The core offer is not specific enough in the primary headline
issues.detail: “Movilidad turística con presencia” is polished positioning language, but it does not immediately tell a procurement or tourism decision-maker what the company supplies or delivers.
issues.evidence: The H1 is “Movilidad turística con presencia.” The service clarification appears later in the supporting paragraph and kicker: “Trenes y tranvías turísticos...” and “Alquiler · venta · proyectos.”
issues.observed: A first-time visitor must interpret the brand and supporting copy before understanding whether the business rents vehicles, sells them, operates services, or designs turnkey projects.
issues.expected: The first viewport should state the concrete category and commercial offer in plain language, with the distinctive proposition supporting it.
issues.recommendation: Use a clearer H1 such as “Trenes y tranvías turísticos para ciudades, eventos y recintos,” then retain “con presencia” as a supporting line or brand proposition.

issues.title: There is insufficient visible proof for a specialist transport provider
issues.detail: The page presents a premium point of view but gives little evidence of delivery capability, installed projects, fleet scale, operating experience, or client relationships.
issues.evidence: The scan identifies only 1 trust signal. The visible hero project brief contains scope information such as Spain and Écija, but no client logos, project outcomes, fleet counts, years of experience, testimonials, or measurable results.
issues.observed: The business claims specialist capability without enough proof to reduce perceived procurement risk.
issues.expected: A credible reference experience would make proof visible early: real project case studies, client or municipality references, operational metrics, and clear fleet/service credentials.
issues.location: Homepage hero and immediately following content.
issues.recommendation: Add a compact proof band below the hero with selected projects, municipalities or clients, years active, number of vehicles/projects, and links to detailed cases. Use the Écija project as a proper case study with images, scope, and outcome.

issues.title: The hero image is too dark and obstructed to function as convincing product proof
issues.detail: The train is recognizable, but the heavy black overlay and dark left-side treatment substantially reduce visible detail. The vehicle is the core commercial asset, yet its body, passenger area, and operating context are difficult to inspect.
issues.evidence: In both screenshots, large areas of the red train are obscured by a near-black overlay; the mobile crop shows mostly dark bodywork behind the text, with limited usable vehicle detail.
issues.observed: The image reads primarily as atmosphere behind typography rather than as evidence of the actual fleet and service.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution would preserve enough contrast and vehicle detail to make the asset feel tangible, capable, and commercially credible while maintaining text legibility.
issues.location: Homepage hero background, desktop and mobile first viewport.
issues.recommendation: Reduce overlay density over the vehicle, use a more intentional gradient only where text requires it, and choose a crop that keeps the full front or passenger section legible. Add a secondary fleet or service image immediately after the hero.

issues.title: The lead path depends entirely on a separate contact page with no qualification signal in the hero
issues.detail: The CTA is visible and functional, but the homepage does not help a prospect understand what information is needed, how quickly they will receive a response, or which enquiry type is appropriate.
issues.evidence: Objective scan reports 0 forms and 0 booking signals. The primary CTA links to `contacto.html`; there is no visible response-time statement, enquiry category, email/phone alternative, or inline qualification mechanism in the first viewport.
issues.observed: The user must commit to another page before knowing whether the company can handle their specific rental, purchase, or project request.
issues.expected: A strong B2B lead path should reduce uncertainty and provide a concise route for selecting project type, destination, dates, vehicle need, or budget context.
issues.location: Hero CTA group and homepage lead journey.
issues.recommendation: Keep the prominent CTA, but add a short qualification form or structured enquiry module on the contact page with project type, location, timing, and message fields. State expected response time and provide a direct contact alternative for urgent enquiries.

issues.title: The mobile hero is too long and pushes essential navigation and proof below the decision point
issues.detail: The mobile layout stacks the headline, paragraph, two full-width buttons, and the entire project brief before the visitor reaches the next section. This increases scrolling before the user sees services or portfolio evidence.
issues.evidence: The mobile screenshot shows the full hero extending through the project brief, with the next section only implied by the bottom progress line. The hero occupies nearly the complete captured page height.
issues.observed: Mobile users receive a long editorial introduction before they can compare services or inspect other vehicles/projects.
issues.expected: The mobile first screen should establish the offer, present one clear CTA, and reveal or quickly lead into the next content section.
issues.recommendation: Shorten the hero copy, collapse the project brief into a compact summary or move it below the first service section, and keep the primary CTA visible without requiring a long scroll.

issues.title: The homepage lacks a strong portfolio narrative after the hero
issues.detail: Portfolio discovery is a stated secondary goal, but the visible opening experience provides only a single project brief and does not immediately demonstrate range or outcomes across the four target contexts.
issues.evidence: The heading structure names four contexts, but the scan reports only 527 words and 1 trust signal. The screenshots show no visible project gallery, client outcomes, or representative fleet range in the first viewport.
issues.observed: The visitor is told about use cases but is not shown enough real work to evaluate fit.
issues.expected: Each context should be supported by a concrete visual case, service outcome, and route into relevant examples.
issues.location: Homepage content following the hero and solution sections.
issues.recommendation: Build a concise portfolio grid or case-study strip using real vehicles and deployments, with location, client type, service delivered, and a clear “Ver caso” action for each.

issues.title: The typography and micro-label system is over-art-directed for a service homepage
issues.detail: The oversized editorial serif headline creates distinction, but it is surrounded by many tiny uppercase labels and fine rules. This produces a high-fashion presentation at the expense of practical scanning and legibility.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports 96 tiny text elements and a tiny-text ratio of 0.38. Desktop navigation is approximately 9.5px, hero kicker 8.5px, and project labels 7.5–8px.
issues.observed: The page feels carefully styled but some navigation, metadata, and contextual labels appear like decorative production notes rather than useful information.
issues.expected: Professional-services pages should retain distinctive typography while keeping navigation, labels, and supporting metadata comfortably readable at normal viewing distance.
issues.location: Header navigation, hero kicker, CTA labels, and “Project Brief / 01” panel.
issues.recommendation: Increase small utility text to a more readable minimum, reduce the number of decorative labels, and reserve uppercase tracking for short eyebrows or section markers only.

issues.title: Mobile interaction and navigation controls are visually small despite the generous layout
issues.detail: The page has ample space but uses very small navigation and utility typography. This makes the experience feel precise at desktop scale but less forgiving on mobile and for users with reduced vision.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports a tiny tap-target ratio of 0.72, with 19 sampled small interactive targets, and a tiny-text ratio of 0.38. The desktop/mobile screenshots show highly compact labels and tightly tracked navigation text.
issues.observed: The hamburger is clear, but surrounding link and metadata treatment is optimized for visual style rather than robust touch and reading comfort.
issues.expected: Mobile controls should have comfortably sized hit areas, readable labels, and clear separation between interactive elements.
issues.location: Header, CTA labels, hero metadata, and mobile menu trigger area.
issues.recommendation: Increase interactive padding and minimum hit areas, raise utility text sizing, and verify focus, hover, and open-menu states at mobile widths.

issues.title: The CTA hierarchy is clear but repetitive and not sufficiently differentiated by intent
issues.detail: “Solicitar presupuesto” is repeated prominently, while “Ver vehículos” is the only secondary path. Different buyer intents such as renting, buying, commissioning a city service, or exploring case studies are not surfaced in the first interaction.
issues.evidence: The hero contains two actions, but the main CTA wording is repeated in the header and hero. The scan reports 2 primary CTA instances and 0 booking signals.
issues.observed: The interface asks most visitors to request a quote before helping them choose the relevant commercial route.
issues.expected: Reference-quality conversion design would preserve one dominant lead action while offering clear, low-friction paths for vehicle discovery and relevant service scenarios.
issues.recommendation: Use “Hablar sobre mi proyecto” or “Solicitar presupuesto” as the single lead action, and pair it with intent-specific links such as “Explorar vehículos,” “Ver proyectos” and “Alquiler para eventos.”

issues.title: Legal and privacy reassurance is missing from the visible site structure
issues.detail: A lead-generation site collecting project enquiries should make business identity, privacy handling, and legal information easy to find before a prospect submits details.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports no privacy link and no legal link. The security/trust score is 75.4, despite the successful HTTP and performance checks.
issues.observed: The absence of visible legal and privacy links weakens trust for municipalities, companies, and other procurement-oriented visitors.
issues.expected: The footer and contact journey should include privacy policy, legal notice, cookie information where applicable, and clear business/contact details.
issues.location: Site footer and contact-page lead journey.
issues.recommendation: Add persistent footer links to legal notice and privacy policy, ensure contact-form consent language is present, and show complete company identification and direct contact details.

issues.title: The page has incomplete image alternative text coverage
issues.detail: The visual experience depends heavily on imagery, so missing alternative text reduces the accessibility and semantic value of important content.
issues.evidence: The scan reports 7 images with a missing-alt ratio of 0.2857 and identifies the YouTube thumbnail and an Écija Wikimedia image as examples.
issues.observed: At least two content images may be announced without useful descriptions or may be skipped semantically, depending on implementation.
issues.expected: Every meaningful image should describe the vehicle, place, project, or operational context; purely decorative backgrounds should be explicitly treated as decorative.
issues.location: Homepage image assets, including the video thumbnail and Écija image.
issues.recommendation: Add concise Spanish alt text that identifies the subject and relevance, and use empty alt only for genuinely decorative assets.

aiReview.summary: A visually distinctive, technically fast homepage with a credible premium direction, but the execution currently favors atmosphere and art direction over service clarity, proof, and lead-generation efficiency. The desktop hero is strong at first glance, while the mobile version becomes long, text-heavy, and difficult to scan. The business is identifiable, but the page does not yet communicate enough evidence that Trenes y Tranvías is an established specialist provider capable of delivering complex transport projects.
strengths: The first viewport clearly establishes a premium, specialist visual identity rather than looking like a generic transport template.
The hero image is relevant to the business and shows an actual tourist train, providing immediate category recognition.
The primary CTA, “Solicitar presupuesto,” is prominent in both desktop and mobile layouts and links consistently to the contact page.
The local signal “Écija · Sevilla” is useful for regional relevance and gives the business a concrete point of origin.
The hero information hierarchy is coherent: category kicker, proposition, explanatory copy, CTA group, and project brief.
The technical foundation is strong: fast loading, no layout shift, no horizontal overflow, valid heading structure, working internal links, and successful critical-journey checks.

issues.detail: The opening experience is almost entirely black, with no visible yacht, sea, marina, guest experience, or destination imagery in either supplied viewport. For a luxury yacht charter, the product and the aspiration must be immediate; currently the hero could belong to an abstract premium service rather than Marbella charter.
issues.evidence: Both desktop and mobile screenshots show a near-black hero field behind all core messaging. The scan records six images site-wide, but none establishes the offer in the first viewport.
issues.expected: Reference-quality luxury charter sites use an exceptional, real, location-specific hero image or video: a yacht in use, recognizable Mediterranean light, and a composition that still permits highly legible enquiry controls.
issues.location: Homepage hero, above the enquiry module
issues.observed: The brand relies on typography and dark atmosphere rather than demonstrable yacht-charter value.
issues.recommendation: Replace the black hero field with art-directed, high-resolution Marbella/Puerto Banus charter imagery or restrained video footage. Preserve the dark type treatment with a carefully judged overlay, but ensure the vessel, water, and premium onboard context remain plainly visible.
issues.title: The primary viewport does not sell the yacht experience visually

issues.detail: The primary conversion surface reads more like a static itinerary summary than a clearly interactive availability search. Only the date has an explicit calendar icon; Guests, Duration, Departure, and The day have no visible chevrons, selected-control treatment, or other cue that they can be changed.
issues.evidence: In both screenshots the values are set in editorial serif text within plain grid cells. The desktop CTA is offset into a dark separate block; on mobile the fifth grid cell is visibly blank beside “The day,” followed by a separate full-width CTA.
issues.expected: A best-in-class enquiry tool makes each configurable field unmistakably actionable, exposes current selection states clearly, and presents one coherent path from inputs to availability/enquiry.
issues.observed: The interaction model is visually ambiguous at the exact moment a visitor should begin configuring a charter.
issues.recommendation: Give every selectable field a consistent disclosure affordance and active/focus state, clarify whether the experience is availability search or bespoke enquiry, and redesign the mobile layout so the final field occupies an intentional full-width row rather than appearing alongside an empty grid area.
issues.title: The charter finder has weak input affordance

issues.detail: The page makes a local-experience claim but supplies no independently legible proof near the conversion decision. “15+ years local experience,” “Real availability,” and “Qualified skipper” are assertions, not trust evidence.
issues.evidence: The DOM scan reports zero trust signals. The screenshots show only self-authored reassurance copy beneath the finder; no review rating, client testimonial, fleet/operator credentials, safety or insurance proof, press recognition, or recognizable partner badges are visible.
issues.expected: Luxury travel buyers should be able to quickly validate who operates the charter, why the service is credible, and what protects a high-value booking before committing to an enquiry.
issues.location: Homepage, directly beneath the charter finder and through the first discovery sections
issues.observed: The site states reasons to trust the business without substantiating them, which lowers confidence for a premium, remote purchase.
issues.recommendation: Add concise, verifiable proof in the decision path: a sourced review rating, operating history with named local basis, skipper/insurance or licensing credentials where accurate, and authentic client or partner evidence. Avoid decorative logo strips or unsupported superlatives.
issues.title: Premium trust is asserted rather than evidenced

issues.detail: The desktop page incurs a very large layout shift, which can move the visitor's chosen target as the initial experience settles.
issues.evidence: Objective measurement reports desktop CLS of 0.7092, far above the 0.1 good threshold; mobile CLS is 0. This is particularly consequential because the shifting region contains the primary charter finder and CTA.
issues.expected: The hero, typography, imagery, booking module, and any late-loading assets should reserve their final dimensions so the above-the-fold journey remains stable.
issues.observed: The otherwise composed desktop experience has an unstable load state that undermines polish and can disrupt interaction.
issues.recommendation: Identify the shifting elements in a performance trace, reserve explicit space for hero media and fonts, stabilize booking-module dimensions, and retest desktop CLS until it is below 0.1.
issues.title: Desktop visual stability falls well below premium standards

issues.detail: The composition is typographically strong but overly dependent on the same dark editorial treatment. The dense black hero, black CTA band, black proof strip, and small pale text create limited material contrast or sense of place.
issues.evidence: Desktop shows successive black regions for the hero, finder CTA, and reassurance row. Mobile extends this into most of the first viewport and below. The site has 38 colors in the scan, yet the supplied journey reads almost monochrome.
issues.expected: A cinematic luxury system can be restrained while still varying visual material, imagery, scale, and pacing to create a richer sense of exclusivity and destination.
issues.location: Homepage hero and immediate post-finder content
issues.observed: The result feels polished but closer to a dark premium web template than a distinct Marbella charter world.
issues.recommendation: Introduce real Mediterranean visual material, controlled lighter editorial intervals, and more specific yacht/departure details in the first journey. Keep the refined typography, but use it as a framing device rather than the sole source of perceived luxury.
issues.title: The first journey feels visually generic for the destination

issues.detail: Pricing context is too narrow and potentially unclear for a high-consideration luxury booking. The only visible price is a small line for one Sunseeker: “from €4,375 / 4h,” followed by “low season · 21% VAT excluded.”
issues.evidence: The desktop reassurance strip contains the sole price cue in small secondary type. It is not paired with fleet comparison, guest capacity, inclusions, seasonality explanation, or an unambiguous all-in estimate.
issues.expected: Users should be able to judge budget fit without having to infer the actual cost structure, while retaining an enquiry-led luxury sales model.
issues.observed: Price is presented as a fine-print fragment rather than decision-supporting information, and VAT exclusion may create avoidable friction after an enquiry starts.
issues.recommendation: Surface a clearer starting-price range and “from” basis near fleet discovery, state key inclusions/exclusions plainly, and make the VAT treatment visible at the point it changes the buyer's expected total.
issues.title: Price framing does not adequately support qualification

issues.detail: Several labels and contact/legal links use very small type, which weakens scanability despite technically adequate target heights.
issues.evidence: The scan identifies ten visible elements at 10.4–11.5px, including the header phone number, footer/legal links, and uppercase labels. On the supplied mobile screenshot, these support details are visibly less comfortable than the main content.
issues.expected: Luxury interfaces may use secondary typography, but commercial contact details and supporting navigation should remain effortlessly readable at common mobile viewing distances.
issues.location: Header contact number, finder labels, and footer/legal links
issues.observed: Essential secondary information recedes to a degree that feels more editorial than service-oriented.
issues.recommendation: Increase the minimum size and contrast of operational text, especially the phone number and legal/navigation links; retain hierarchy through weight and spacing rather than sub-12px copy.

aiReview.summary: This is a polished and structurally capable luxury-charter homepage whose typography and conversion prominence outperform most generic charter sites. It stops short of reference quality because the most important visual and commercial proof is absent in the first decision path: visitors cannot see the actual charter experience, have limited reason to trust the operator beyond its own claims, and face an availability tool with ambiguous controls. The desktop layout-shift score also materially conflicts with the intended premium finish.
strengths: The visual system has disciplined typography, generous whitespace, and a credible premium tone rather than discount-charter styling.
The headline is specific to Marbella/Puerto Banus and creates a concise, memorable geographic proposition.
The enquiry journey is placed immediately below the hero and is reinforced with a prominent desktop CTA plus mobile Plan a charter and WhatsApp actions.
Navigation, fleet, experiences, destinations, owners, and contact provide a logical discovery structure; the scan confirms no broken internal links and a working form path.
Mobile has no horizontal overflow, strong measured load performance, and a clear menu/contact treatment.

aiReview.summary: Marbella For Sale has a strong luxury visual premise and excellent underlying delivery, but the first impression prioritizes atmosphere and brand treatment over legibility, immediate property discovery and buyer confidence. The most valuable next step is to make the hero work as a real acquisition surface: readable proposition, unambiguous discovery CTA, discreet search access and tangible proof of local advisory expertise.
strengths: The cinematic villa imagery, restrained palette and expansive hero scale are directionally appropriate for Marbella luxury real estate.
The layout is technically stable and responsive: the scan reports no horizontal overflow, zero CLS, complete image alt coverage and strong mobile performance.
The information architecture is broad and relevant, with properties, developments, areas, selling, insights and contact routes represented.
Navigation, heading order and form labeling are structurally sound, so the principal weaknesses are prioritization and visible craft rather than basic usability failures.

issues.detail: The mandatory privacy layer is the dominant first-screen interaction and interrupts the reservation journey before the guest can assess the venue or act.
issues.evidence: Desktop screenshot: the privacy modal covers the lower-right hero and obscures the likely primary action area. Mobile screenshot: it occupies roughly the lower 40% of the viewport, covering the headline and below-the-fold continuation. The primary goal is reservation.
issues.expected: A reference-quality premium restaurant should keep legal consent compliant while preserving immediate access to the reservation path and first-impression storytelling.
issues.location: Homepage hero, desktop and mobile first viewport
issues.observed: The large, high-contrast cookie panel competes more strongly than the restaurant content; its “ENTENDIDO” button is more visually assertive than the visible reservation control.
issues.recommendation: Use a compact, bottom-anchored technical-cookie notice with a single acknowledgement and a discreet policy link, or defer nonessential detail to a secondary layer. Ensure the fixed mobile reservation action remains visible and independently tappable while consent is shown.
issues.title: Cookie consent overwhelms the first reservation opportunity

issues.detail: Reservation choices are fragmented at desktop scale, creating unnecessary decision-making at the moment the business should present one clear next step.
issues.evidence: The desktop header shows both “CONSULTAR RESERVA” and “RESERVAR”, alongside a phone number. The scan records 7 primary CTAs and 5 booking signals on one homepage, and an inconsistent-button ratio of 0.407.

issues.recommendation: Make “Reservar” the sole primary header CTA. Move the consultation route into the booking flow or label it specifically for private events/groups. Keep phone contact subordinate, for example in a contact menu or footer.
issues.title: Booking hierarchy is diluted by competing CTAs

issues.detail: The award claim appears without enough visible context to function as a credible premium trust signal.
issues.evidence: Mobile screenshot places “BEST OF THE BEST 2025” prominently beneath the header, but no awarding organization, badge, source, or explanatory context is visible. The scan identifies only one trust signal overall.
issues.expected: A reference-quality restaurant presentation makes third-party acclaim verifiable and specific, especially when it is promoted in the most valuable screen space.
issues.observed: The claim reads as a generic marketing label rather than proof. It also receives more visual emphasis than tangible reasons to choose the restaurant, such as cuisine, view, menu, or guest recognition.
issues.recommendation: Name and visually identify the awarding authority, such as TripAdvisor where applicable, with a genuine badge or source-linked citation. Place it near concise social proof or below the hero rather than using it as an unsupported standalone line.
issues.title: Prominent accolade lacks visible attribution

issues.detail: The hero imagery is atmospheric and aligned to waterfront dining, but the mobile crop prioritizes furniture and glassware over a clearly appetising food or service moment.

issues.title: Mobile hero underdelivers on appetite and product proof

aiReview.summary: La Bocana has a high-quality visual foundation and unusually strong operational baseline for a restaurant site. It is not reference-quality yet because the first-view consent interruption, split booking hierarchy, unsupported award treatment, and over-varied action system reduce the effortless confidence expected in Puerto Banús premium dining. Resolve the consent and CTA hierarchy first; these changes directly improve the reservation journey without changing the brand direction.
strengths: The hero establishes a credible Puerto Banús waterfront setting immediately, with a warm, editorial photographic direction that suits a premium Mediterranean restaurant.

Brand, location, language access, telephone contact, menu route, and reservation route are all present. The scan confirms working internal links, no broken paths, clear heading structure, and strong location/contact coverage.

The underlying experience is technically polished: fast load metrics, zero layout shift, no horizontal overflow, accessible target sizing, complete image alt coverage, and no observed console or request failures.
The desktop and mobile navigation make reservation visible without relying on a hidden menu alone; the mobile header gives booking meaningful prominence.

issues.location: Global page styling, especially header and hero
issues.observed: The first viewport feels broken or unfinished rather than editorial, aspirational or credible. The primary message is effectively inaccessible at a glance.
issues.recommendation: Correct the foreground/background contrast first. Use a clearly legible light-on-dark or dark-on-light system, verify contrast on every text style, and establish distinct treatments for the logo, navigation, H1, supporting copy and calls to action.
issues.title: First-viewport content is effectively unreadable

issues.detail: The homepage does not visually demonstrate the core product: properties for sale or rent in Écija. It presents an abstract text introduction without showing homes, spaces, locations or current inventory.
issues.evidence: The screenshot contains no visible property imagery or listing modules. The objective scan reports imageCount 0 and only 57 words on the document.
issues.expected: Premium real estate positioning requires the actual inventory and local market to be the first-viewport signal, with high-quality photography, property type, location and key facts visible immediately.
issues.location: Homepage hero and content immediately below it
issues.observed: A visitor cannot assess the quality, style or relevance of the agency's portfolio without navigating elsewhere, and the page provides no emotional or commercial reason to continue.
issues.recommendation: Lead with a curated property discovery module: large, high-quality local imagery, price, type, area, location and availability. Add a clear route into the complete inventory while preserving a restrained editorial composition.
issues.title: The homepage does not showcase the real estate offering

issues.detail: There is no meaningful enquiry mechanism in the homepage experience. The primary conversion path appears to be a generic Contacto link, with no visible form, property-specific enquiry action, phone action or contextual lead capture.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports formCount 0, primaryCtaCount 1 and only one contact signal, the generic Contacto link. bookingSignalCount is 0.
issues.expected: The critical journey is property enquiry. Reference-quality execution gives visitors a low-friction way to request information, arrange a viewing or speak to the agency, ideally from both the homepage and each property detail page.
issues.observed: The user must make an additional navigation decision before they can enquire, and the CTA does not communicate what happens after clicking.
issues.recommendation: Add a prominent, specific CTA such as “Ver inmuebles” plus a secondary “Solicitar información” or “Concertar visita”. Include a short enquiry form with property, name, phone/email and preferred contact method, alongside click-to-call contact on mobile.
issues.title: The primary property-enquiry journey is underdeveloped

issues.detail: Property discovery is not available as an immediate workflow. The visible page offers no search controls, category entry points, featured inventory, or summary of available stock.
issues.evidence: The screenshots show only text navigation and introductory copy. The scan identifies internal links to /inmuebles but no form controls and no visible discovery interface on the homepage.
issues.expected: Visitors should be able to start browsing by intent, such as buying, renting, property type, area or budget, with a clear result count and useful filters on the inventory page.
issues.observed: “Inmuebles” is a destination link rather than a useful discovery step. The page does not help users understand what is available or how to narrow the search.
issues.recommendation: Add featured or latest properties to the homepage and make the inventory route explicit. Provide filters for operation, type, municipality, price and bedrooms, with strong mobile controls and persistent query state.
issues.title: Property discovery is reduced to a bare navigation link

issues.detail: The supplied page has no visual assets and therefore cannot deliver the editorial or aspirational qualities expected from premium real estate. The absence is especially damaging because property imagery is the primary way visitors evaluate fit and perceived value.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports imageCount 0. Both screenshots show a flat background with no property photography, location imagery, floor plans, maps or branded visual detail.
issues.expected: Use real, well-lit property photography with consistent art direction and thoughtful crops. Imagery should reveal the actual homes and local environment rather than act as generic decoration.
issues.location: Homepage hero and property discovery content
issues.observed: The experience feels like a text placeholder or incomplete prototype, not a premium agency storefront.
issues.recommendation: Commission or curate a small set of authentic Écija property images. Use one strong hero property or local architectural image, then support it with a disciplined listing grid and consistent image ratios.
issues.title: No imagery supports the premium real-estate promise

issues.detail: The design language does not currently communicate premium real estate. The restrained burgundy background could support a sophisticated identity, but the execution lacks the contrast, composition, imagery, spacing and detail needed to make it feel intentional.
issues.evidence: The screenshots show a largely empty monochrome page with low-contrast text and no property media. The visible element count is only 22, and the page has no apparent visual content system.
issues.expected: Premium should feel calm and selective, with strong art direction, precise typography, generous but purposeful spacing, clear content sequencing and tangible evidence of quality.
issues.observed: The page reads closer to an unstyled or failed-render state than a finished luxury brand experience.
issues.recommendation: Rebuild the first viewport around one clear composition: legible brand/navigation, a property-led visual, a direct value proposition, and a high-intent CTA. Follow with inventory, local expertise and proof rather than leaving most of the viewport empty.
issues.title: The visual execution sits below the stated positioning

issues.detail: The mobile navigation links are smaller than comfortable touch targets. The issue is not horizontal overflow, but interaction confidence and spacing on a device where browsing and calling are high-value actions.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports tinyTapTargetCount 9 of 10 interactive targets, with all sampled links measuring approximately 21px high.
issues.expected: Mobile navigation and utility actions should have generous hit areas, clear separation and an intentional menu treatment when the full navigation no longer fits comfortably.
issues.observed: The navigation appears as small text links with insufficient vertical hit area, which makes repeated mobile browsing less ergonomic.
issues.recommendation: Increase link hit areas to approximately 44px minimum, add horizontal and vertical spacing, and use a properly labelled menu or compact navigation pattern where needed. Make phone and enquiry actions especially easy to reach.
issues.title: Mobile navigation targets are too small

issues.detail: The content is too sparse to support premium positioning, local expertise or purchase confidence. The headline makes a useful local promise, but the page provides almost no supporting proof, inventory context or service differentiation.
issues.evidence: The scan reports 57 total words, trustSignalCount 0 and no visible testimonials, credentials, market facts, service explanation or team proof in the supplied screenshots.
issues.expected: The page should quickly explain why Noguera is credible in Écija and Sevilla, what kinds of property it handles, how it supports buyers and sellers, and why a visitor should make contact.
issues.observed: The copy states that the search is clearer but does not substantiate that claim. There is no evidence of expertise, track record, process or service quality.
issues.recommendation: Add concise proof-oriented sections: local market expertise, buyer and seller services, a transparent valuation process, selected client feedback, agency credentials and practical Écija-specific guidance. Keep the writing concise and avoid generic real-estate claims.
issues.title: The value proposition is asserted but not substantiated

issues.detail: The visible experience does not surface the basic legal and privacy signals expected from a Spanish property business collecting or intending to collect leads.
issues.evidence: The objective scan reports hasPrivacyLink false and hasLegalLink false. The screenshots show no footer trust or legal area.

aiReview.summary: The site has a useful local premise and strong baseline technical performance, but the supplied experience is not commercially or visually ready for premium real estate. The near-unreadable contrast, complete absence of property imagery, extremely thin content and missing homepage enquiry path prevent visitors from seeing the product, trusting the agency or taking the primary action. The first priority is to make the homepage legible and property-led, then add discovery and a specific, low-friction enquiry journey.
strengths: The proposition is locally specific, naming Écija rather than using entirely generic real-estate language.
The H1 is unique and structurally valid, and the navigation exposes relevant routes for properties, selling, guides and contact.
The page is technically lightweight and stable according to the scan: 396ms desktop LCP, 536ms mobile LCP, 0.0012 CLS and no failed network requests or console errors.
The scan reports no horizontal overflow, valid viewport metadata, working internal links, a valid robots file and sitemap, and complete image alt coverage for the assets that currently exist.
